title: Meet input(): ask the user
idea: input() pauses the program, lets the user type, and hands back what they typed as a string. Meet it with visible behavior.

options: Pauses and waits for the user to type something, then gives it back
exercises.explanation: input() is how a program ASKS. It waits for the user to type and press Enter, then hands the typed text back.

exercises.prompt:
Where does the typed answer go in this line?

name = input("Your name: ")
exercises.explanation: Whatever the user types is stored in name, so a later line can use it. input() gives back a value; = remembers it.

exercises.prompt: What is the text in the brackets, as in input("Your name: ")?
options: A prompt shown to the user before they type
exercises.explanation: The string inside input() is the prompt - it tells the user what to type. It is displayed first, then the program waits.

exercises.prompt: What TYPE of value does input() always give back?
options: A string (text), even if the user types digits
exercises.explanation: input() always returns text. Even if the user types 5, you get the string "5". This matters a lot - next lessons cover it.

exercises.prompt:
The user runs this and types Ada:

name = input("Your name: ")
print("Hello " + name)

What appears after they type?
exercises.explanation: name holds "Ada", and "Hello " + name joins them into "Hello Ada". (Concatenation review.)

exercises.prompt: input() makes the program wait until the user presses Enter.
exercises.explanation: Yes - the program pauses at input() until the user finishes typing and hits Enter. Then it continues with the typed value.

exercises.prompt:
Order the steps when this runs:

city = input("City? ")
print("Nice, " + city)
blocks: Wait for the user to type and press Enter
Store what they typed in city
exercises.explanation: Prompt, wait, store, then use. That is the lifecycle of an input() call.

exercises.prompt: Why is input() powerful compared to a fixed value in the code?
options: The program can react to different answers each time it runs
exercises.explanation: Instead of a value baked in, the program responds to whatever the user types - so it behaves differently for different people.

exercises.prompt:
Fill the tool that asks the user for text:

answer = ____("Type yes or no: ")
exercises.explanation: input() shows the prompt, waits, and returns the typed text into answer.

options: It brings the user's typed answer into the program as a string
exercises.explanation: input() is the doorway for user answers. Next, you will branch on those answers to react to them.
